records.title: East India Company territorial government
records.dateNote: The company was chartered on 31 December 1600 as a trading body. This entry starts at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, which the article calls the beginning of its transformation into a colonial power, and ends when the Government of India Act was passed on 2 August 1858. The company remained a legal entity until 1873. Trade before 1757 is not treated as rule of the subcontinent.
records.summary: The English company’s period of territorial government in India, from Plassey to the transfer of that government to the Crown.

citations.locator: Opening; Control of India; Decline and loss of power
citations.supports: Charter, Plassey, presidencies and the loss of political control.
The Act of 2 August 1858 transferred British power in India from the company to the Crown.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Not a dynasty. A chartered English company, formally the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies and, from 1708, the United Company of Merchants of England Trading to the East Indies. It acted as an agent of British imperialism.

citations.supports: Corporate identity rather than a royal house.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: Three presidencies are named: Bengal, Madras and Bombay. Madras grew from a fortification of 1639. Calcutta, founded in 1690, became the centre of the company’s commercial and political power. A governor-general later became the centre of authority. There was no single indigenous capital of “India” under the company.

citations.supports: Presidencies and Calcutta.

details.heading: Rulers and reigns
details.text: Robert Clive commanded the troops at Plassey. The article does not make him a sovereign. Political oversight moved, by the Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt’s India Act of 1784, toward a British government board. From 1834 the company was “merely a managing agency” for that government.

citations.supports: Clive, the Acts and the 1834 change.

details.heading: Events
details.text: Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) opened Company control in Bengal and Bihar. Shah Alam II then granted the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Mysore Wars, Maratha Wars (1775–82, 1803–05, 1817–18) and Sikh Wars (1845–46 and 1848–49) are the campaigns named. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 ended the company’s political role.

citations.supports: Battles, diwani, wars and 1857.

details.heading: Culture, religion and economy
details.text: The article describes revenue collection, the decline of Indian textile crafts, a severe land tax, and the Bengal famine of 1770, which it calls a direct result of harsh revenue policy. It also records a judiciary, a postal service, the start of railway construction in 1850, missionary education and the abolition of sati. From the 1620s to the 1770s the company transported enslaved people, mostly from East Africa. Princely states kept nominal autonomy under treaties and residents while submitting to company political authority.

citations.locator: Economic and social impact; Role as enslavers; princely-state sentences
citations.supports: Revenue, famine, institutions, enslavement and indirect rule.

records.locationNote: Timeline-only record: a source-verified map coordinate has not yet been attached. No territorial extent or personal location is implied.
records.title: British raj
records.dateNote: Britannica dates direct Crown rule from 1858 until the independence of India and Pakistan in 1947. Parliament passed the Government of India Act on 2 August 1858. The Indian Independence Act sets up the two Dominions on 15 August 1947, so 1947 is both the raj’s last year and the Dominions’ first. Provincial borders are not drawn by this entry.
records.summary: Direct British Crown government of the Indian subcontinent from the 1858 Act to independence in 1947.

citations.locator: Introduction; Government of India Act of 1858
citations.supports: The 1858–1947 span and the Act of 2 August 1858.
Two independent Dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Not a dynasty. The Crown replaced the company. A secretary of state for India sat in the British cabinet. Day-to-day control remained with viceroys and the Indian Civil Service. In 1876 Queen Victoria took the title Empress of India.

citations.locator: Government of India Act of 1858; Social policy
citations.supports: Secretary of state, viceroy and the imperial title.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: Viceroys divided their time between Calcutta and Simla. The article later names New Delhi as the new capital city of British India. It does not give the year of the move in the passage used.

citations.locator: Government of India Act; Prelude to independence
citations.supports: Calcutta, Simla and New Delhi.

details.heading: Rulers and reigns
details.text: Viceroys named in the passages used include Canning (1856–62), Northbrook (1872–76), Lytton (1876–80), Ripon (1880–84), Lansdowne (1888–94), Elgin (1894–99) and Curzon (1899–1905). These are office-holders, not kings of an Indian dynasty. The list is not complete.

citations.supports: Named viceroys and their stated dates.

details.heading: Events
details.text: The 1857 rebellion is the article’s immediate background. Victoria’s proclamation was announced by Canning on 1 November 1858. The Indian National Congress first met in December 1885. The Muslim League was founded in 1906. The article carries the story through partition in 1947. Independence created two Dominions, not one successor state.

citations.locator: Introduction; Social policy; Congress; partition narrative
citations.supports: Rebellion, proclamation, Congress, the League and 1947.
The two Dominions and the appointed day.

details.heading: Culture, religion and economy
details.text: The 1858 proclamation promised support for “native princes” and non-interference in religious belief. Land revenue, a salt monopoly and the opium trade to China are named as fiscal pillars. Railways grew from barely 200 miles in 1858. Famine, commercial crops and the decline of handicrafts are part of the same economic account. More than 560 princely enclaves remained outside the directly ruled provinces.

citations.supports: Princes, revenue, railways and famine.

records.locationNote: Timeline-only record: a source-verified map coordinate has not yet been attached. No territorial extent or personal location is implied.
records.title: Princely states under Crown paramountcy
records.dateNote: From Victoria’s proclamation of 1 November 1858 through the “nine decades of crown rule” in which the article says more than 560 princely enclaves remained. This is a class of many states, not one kingdom and not a map of each state. The 1935 Act’s federation with the princes was never realized. Individual states need their own records.
records.summary: Hundreds of indirectly ruled states whose princes swore allegiance to the British Crown after 1858.

citations.locator: Social policy; Government of India Act of 1935
citations.supports: The proclamation, the count of enclaves and the failed federation.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Many dynasties. The article does not merge them. Earlier Company treaties had already put princely states under indirect rule; the 1858 proclamation reversed Dalhousie’s annexation policy and promised continued support for princes who swore allegiance.

citations.supports: Many states, and the change from annexation.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: No shared capital. Each court had its own seat. The viceroy’s Foreign Department handled relations with them.

citations.supports: No common capital; the Foreign Department.

details.heading: Rulers and reigns
details.text: Princes could adopt heirs if they swore allegiance. This entry does not list those rulers. Rajput and other houses already in the catalogue keep their own dates.

citations.supports: Adoption and allegiance, without a combined king list.

details.heading: Events
details.text: The article says most important princes did not join the 1857 rebellion. In 1935 a planned federation of provinces and princely states failed because the princes could not agree. Accession of each state after 1947 is not dated by this source.

citations.supports: 1857 and the failed federation. Later accession is outside this citation.

details.heading: Culture, religion and economy
details.text: The proclamation promised non-interference in religious belief. The states are described as autocratic enclaves inside British India. Their economies are not surveyed here. They must not be coloured as one cultural region.

citations.supports: Religious non-interference and the political form.

records.locationNote: Timeline-only record: a source-verified map coordinate has not yet been attached. No territorial extent or personal location is implied.
records.title: Dominion of India
records.dateNote: Section 1 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 sets up a Dominion named India on 15 August 1947, alongside Pakistan. The search window runs to 2026 so the successor state remains discoverable. This citation does not date a republican constitution, internal state borders, or who held office in a given year. It is not a kingdom, and elected leaders are not listed as rulers.
records.summary: The state named India created as a Dominion on 15 August 1947. Later constitutional change is outside this citation.

citations.supports: The appointed day and the name of the Dominion.
Independence of India and Pakistan in 1947 as the end of the raj.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: None. The Act creates a Dominion, not a royal house. Partition created two Dominions. This record follows only the one named India.

citations.supports: Dominion status and the separate Dominion of Pakistan.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: The Act’s section 1 does not name a capital. The raj article calls New Delhi the new capital of British India before independence. That is not restated here as a 1947 legal capital.

citations.supports: No capital is enacted in this section.
New Delhi as the late-raj capital, not as a section of the Act.

details.heading: Rulers and reigns
details.text: No ruler is attached. Office-holders after 1947 need their own sources and are not kings.

citations.supports: The Act names the Dominion and not a monarch of India.

details.heading: Events
details.text: The appointed day is 15 August 1947. The same Act is the legal end of the raj entry. Communal violence and mass migration are described in the raj article’s partition narrative and are not given as a single map layer here.

citations.supports: The appointed day.
The article’s account of partition violence, without a boundary file.

details.heading: Culture, religion and economy
details.text: Not established by the Act. The Dominion was a constitutional state containing many religious communities. A modern outline on a historical sheet is still not a claim about culture or about the borders of 1947.

citations.supports: The section is a constitutional provision, not a cultural or economic description.

records.title: Ellora caves
records.dateNote: The page’s opening and criterion (iii) describe an uninterrupted sequence of monuments from 600 to 1000. The brief synthesis also says rock-cut work ran in three phases from the 6th century to the 12th century. Those statements are not reconciled here. The 600–1000 window follows the opening sequence. It is not a claim that carving continued in every year, or that one dynasty ruled the site throughout.
records.summary: Rock-cut monasteries and temples at Ellora, with sanctuaries of Buddhism, Brahmanism and Jainism.
records.locationNote: Converted from the UNESCO property reference N20 1 35.004 E75 10 45.012. The point locates the cave group near Aurangabad, not a kingdom and not a single cave.

citations.locator: Opening description; property coordinates N20 1 35.004 E75 10 45.012
citations.supports: The 600–1000 sequence, the three religious sanctuaries, the place near Aurangabad, and the property reference point.

details.heading: What was made
details.text: Thirty-four monasteries and temples were cut side by side into a basalt cliff. The brief synthesis separates an early Buddhist group, a Brahmanical group including the Kailasa temple (cave 16), and a later Jaina group.

citations.locator: Opening; Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis
citations.supports: The number of monuments, the cliff, and the three religious phases including cave 16.

records.title: Monuments at Mahabalipuram
records.dateNote: The opening dates the sanctuaries to the 7th and 8th centuries. The brief synthesis says the Pallavas ruled this area between the 6th and 9th centuries and names Narasimhavarman Rajasimha’s reign as 638–660 for one excavated well. The search window follows the opening’s two centuries, not a foundation year and not continuous building. No property coordinate was copied from the page in this pass, so nothing is placed on the map.
records.summary: Rock-cut and structural temples on the Coromandel coast, founded by the Pallava kings.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The page locates the group on the Coromandel coast and names Mahabalipuram, but this pass did not copy a property coordinate, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Pallava foundation, the Coromandel coast, and the 7th–8th century dating of the sanctuaries.

details.heading: What stands there
details.text: The opening names rathas, mandapas, open-air reliefs including the Descent of the Ganges, and the Shore temple. The brief synthesis calls Mahabalipuram a Pallava port and divides the monuments into caves, monolithic rathas, reliefs, structural temples and excavated remains.

citations.locator: Opening; Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis
citations.supports: The monument types and the port-city description.

records.title: Harsha
records.dateNote: Britannica gives the reign as 606 to 647 and the death as about 647. The end year is that approximate death, not a recorded day. Born about 590 is not the start of the reign. The directly ruled area is described as smaller than the list of kingdoms he warred against.
records.summary: Ruler of a large north Indian realm from 606, with his capital moved to Kannauj.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: The reign years, the move of the capital to Kannauj, and the caution that direct control was smaller than the claimed hegemony.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: He was the second son of Prabhakaravardhana, king of Sthanvishvara (Thanesar). He was crowned after the assassination of his elder brother Rajyavardhana. The article does not set out a successor.

citations.supports: Parentage, Thanesar, and the succession after Rajyavardhana.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: After securing his position he declared himself sovereign of Kannauj, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, and formally transferred his capital there. No coordinate is given.

citations.supports: The transfer of the capital to Kannauj.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: He ruled from 606 to 647. He allied with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa and fought Shashanka of Gauda. An attempt on the Deccan, about 620, was stopped at the Narmada by the Chalukya ruler Pulakeshin II. The article says the area directly under his control was probably no more than modern Uttar Pradesh with parts of Punjab and Rajasthan, even where influence reached further.

citations.supports: The dates, the Narmada check, and the limit on direct control.

details.heading: Culture and religion
details.text: He is described as a Buddhist convert in a Hindu era. Xuanzang depicts him as a Mahayana Buddhist, while the earlier part of the reign is said to have supported orthodox Hinduism. He patronised Bana and Mayura and is credited with three Sanskrit plays. These are literary and religious notes, not a map of belief.

citations.supports: The religious description, Xuanzang, and the named literary patronage.

records.title: Ahom rule in Assam
records.dateNote: The article says the Ahom ruled much of Assam from the 13th century until British rule in 1838. The year 1201 is only the start of a 13th-century search window, not a foundation date. The year 1838 is the cited end of their rule. The window does not mean they held the same territory in every year.
records.summary: A dynasty that ruled much of Assam from the 13th century until British rule in 1838.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article names Assam and does not give a coordinate or a capital point, so nothing is placed on the map. Assam is not drawn as their border.

citations.supports: Rule over much of Assam from the 13th century until British rule in 1838.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: The article calls the Ahom a tribe that originated in Yunnan and later spoke Assamese, their earlier language being extinct. It does not list a full genealogy.

citations.supports: The Yunnan origin and the later use of Assamese.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: Their power in Assam is said to have reached its peak under King Rudra Singh, 1696–1714. That reign is a separate record. This entry is the longer span only.

citations.supports: The peak under Rudra Singh and the 1696–1714 dates.

details.heading: Events
details.text: The cited end is the establishment of British rule in 1838. No battle or border is described on this page.

citations.supports: 1838 as the end of Ahom rule in the article.

records.title: Rudra Singh
records.dateNote: The article gives these years as the reign in which Ahom power in Assam reached its peak. It does not describe the start or end as a particular day, or name a capital.
records.summary: Ahom king during the years the article calls the peak of their power in Assam.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is given for Rudra Singh or for a capital, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The reign 1696–1714 as the peak of Ahom power in Assam.

records.title: Quit India movement
records.dateNote: The movement was launched on 8 August 1942 at a Congress meeting in Bombay. Protests had largely died down by the end of 1942 and the article says the movement was definitively over by March 1943. The window is that campaign, not a claim that protest filled every day, and not independence itself.
records.summary: A mass campaign launched by Gandhi in August 1942 demanding an immediate end to British rule. It did not achieve that end.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The launch meeting was in Bombay, present-day Mumbai, and protests spread widely. The page does not give a coordinate, so no point is shown. Bombay is not the extent of the campaign.

citations.supports: The 8 August 1942 launch in Bombay, the demand to end British rule, and the statement that the campaign did not force immediate decolonisation.

details.heading: Events
details.text: On 8 August 1942 the Congress meeting in Bombay adopted the campaign and Gandhi gave the “Do or Die” appeal. Congress leaders were then arrested. The article describes both nonviolent protest and attacks on railways, post offices and police stations, and a harsh British response. It says at least 1,000 Indians were killed and about 60,000 arrested by the end of 1943.

citations.locator: Opening; Preparations for protest; Protests and reprisals
citations.supports: The Bombay meeting, the arrests, the scale of protest, and the casualty and arrest figures as stated.

details.heading: What this was not
details.text: The movement did not end British rule. Independence and partition came in 1947 and are separate records. Gandhi, Nehru and other leaders named here were not kings, and this entry does not give them a reign.

citations.supports: The campaign’s failure to force immediate decolonisation, and its place in the longer independence struggle.

records.title: Republic of India
records.dateNote: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and went into effect on 26 January 1950. The search window starts at 1950, the year it took effect, and runs to 2026 so the republic remains findable. The end year is the atlas limit, not a constitutional end. This is not a list of presidents or prime ministers, and it is not a map of state borders.
records.summary: The Constitution took effect on 26 January 1950 and established India as a democratic republic and a union of states.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. A constitution is not a coordinate and not a border. No point is shown.

citations.supports: The 26 January 1950 commencement, and the description of India as a democratic republic and a union of states.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: None. The Constitution creates a republic. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the drafting committee and is not a monarch. Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly and later became the first president; that office is not a reign in this atlas.

citations.supports: Ambedkar’s role as drafting-committee chair and Prasad’s role as assembly president.

details.heading: Events
details.text: Adoption was on 26 November 1949. Commencement was on 26 January 1950, now marked as Republic Day. When it took effect, the Constitution repealed nearly all existing legislation, including the Indian Independence Act 1947. The Dominion record covers the 1947 Act and is not replaced by this one.

citations.supports: The adoption and commencement dates, Republic Day, and the repeal of the 1947 Act.

details.heading: Rulers and reigns
details.text: No ruler is attached. Elected and appointed office-holders need their own sources and are not listed as kings.

citations.supports: The text defines a republic and the structure of government, not a royal house.

details.heading: Culture, religion and economy
details.text: The preamble is described as emphasising a secular and democratic state and the aims of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Fundamental rights are grouped in six categories. None of that is a map of culture or of the economy.

citations.locator: Top questions on fundamental rights and the preamble
citations.supports: The secular democratic description and the six groups of fundamental rights.

records.title: Maitrakas of Valabhi
records.dateNote: The article says the dynasty ruled Gujarat and Saurashtra from the 5th to the 8th century. The year 401 only opens a 5th-century search window. It is not Bhatarka’s accession. The end, about 780, is the date given for the killing of Shiladitya VI and the razing of the capital. The window is not continuous rule of a fixed territory.
records.summary: A dynasty in Gujarat and Saurashtra with its capital at Valabhi, independent in practice even when early kings were loosely feudatory to the Guptas.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: The region, the capital, the 5th-to-8th-century span, and the end about 780.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Bhatarka, a general, founded the line as Gupta power decayed. Early kings were loosely feudatory to the Guptas and in fact independent. Shiladitya I, about the late 6th century, is named as a powerful king whose rule extended into Malwa and Rajasthan. Shiladitya VI is named as the last king.

citations.supports: The founder, the Gupta relationship, Shiladitya I, and Shiladitya VI.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: The kingdom suffered at the hands of the Chalukyas of the Deccan and of Harsha of Kannauj, then revived after Harsha’s death. Arabs established in Sindh in 712 killed Shiladitya VI and razed Valabhi about 780.

citations.supports: The Chalukya and Harsha pressure, and the Arab attack of about 780.

details.heading: Culture and religion
details.text: The kings patronised religious foundations. The kingdom was an important Buddhist centre, and tradition places the codification of the Shvetambara Jaina canon at Valabhi. That tradition is reported as tradition, not as a dated inscription.

citations.supports: Patronage, Buddhism, and the Jaina tradition.

records.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj
records.dateNote: This record follows the line of Nagabhata, which the article places at Ujjain and later Kannauj from the 8th to the 11th centuries. The year 701 only opens an 8th-century search window. The year 1018 is when Mahmud of Ghazna drove Rajyapala from Kannauj. A separate Harichandra line at Mandor, mostly feudatory, is not this record. Much of the empire was held through vassals.
records.summary: The main Pratihara line of northern India, with its later capital at Kannauj, from the 8th century until Rajyapala was driven out in 1018.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.locator: Opening and narrative of the Nagabhata line
citations.supports: The two lines, the Kannauj capital, the 8th-to-11th-century span, and Rajyapala’s expulsion in 1018.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Nagabhata I, in the 8th century, is the founder of the later line and appears to have ruled in Malwa. His grandnephew Vatsaraja is attested as king of Ujjain in 783 and was defeated by the Rashtrakutas. Nagabhata II captured Kannauj from Chakrayudha about 816 and made it his capital.

citations.supports: Nagabhata I, Vatsaraja in 783, and the capture of Kannauj about 816.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: Under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala (about 890–910) the empire is said to have rivalled the Guptas in extent, from Gujarat and Kathiawar to northern Bengal, much of it loosely held. After Mahendrapala the succession is obscure. Indra III of the Rashtrakutas sacked Kannauj about 916. By the end of the 10th century the Pratiharas controlled little more than the Gangetic doab.

citations.supports: The peak, the loose hold, the 916 sack, and the later shrinkage.

details.heading: Events
details.text: Rajyapala, the last important king, was driven from Kannauj by Mahmud of Ghazna in 1018 and later killed by the forces of the Chandela king Vidyadhara. A small principality apparently survived near Allahabad for about a generation. That survival is described as apparent, not as a mapped remnant.

citations.supports: 1018, Vidyadhara, and the uncertain later principality.

records.title: Mihira Bhoja
records.dateNote: The article says Mihira Bhoja succeeded about 836. It gives Mahendrapala, called Bhoja’s successor, a reign of about 890–910. The year 890 is that successor’s cited start, not a separately recorded death date for Bhoja.
records.summary: Pratihara king under whom, with his successor, the empire reached its peak.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: Accession about 836 and the peak shared with Mahendrapala.

records.title: Mahendrapala
records.dateNote: The article gives this reign as about 890–910. Both ends are approximate. In his time the loosely held territory is said to have reached from Gujarat and Kathiawar to northern Bengal.
records.summary: Pratihara king during the years the article calls the empire’s greatest extent.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: The reign of about 890–910 and the stated reach.

records.title: Temples at Khajuraho
records.dateNote: The opening says the temples were built during the Chandella dynasty, which reached its apogee between 950 and 1050. The brief synthesis says the Chandellas ruled the region in the 10th and 11th centuries. The window follows the apogee dates in the opening. It is not a claim that every temple was begun in 950 or finished in 1050. This pass did not copy a property coordinate.
records.summary: A group of Hindu and Jain temples built while the Chandella dynasty was at its height.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: Chandella patronage, the 950–1050 apogee, and the Hindu and Jain temples.

details.heading: What stands there
details.text: About 20 temples remain, in three groups. The Temple of Kandariya is singled out for its sculpture. The brief synthesis counts 23 temples, including one partly excavated structure, in western, eastern and southern clusters, and calls them Nagara-style.

citations.locator: Opening; Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis
citations.supports: The surviving temples, the clusters, and the Nagara description.

records.title: Temples at Pattadakal
records.dateNote: The opening places the monuments in the 7th and 8th centuries under the Chalukya dynasty. The year 601 opens the 7th-century window and is not a foundation date. Queen Lokamahadevi’s Virupaksha temple is dated about 740. No property coordinate was copied.
records.summary: Nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary at Pattadakal, in Karnataka, from the Chalukya period.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.supports: The Chalukya dating, the temple count, and the Virupaksha temple of about 740.

records.title: Qutb Minar and its monuments
records.dateNote: The brief synthesis says a minar was built at the south-eastern corner of the Quwwatu’l-Islam between 1199 and 1503, and dates Alauddin Khalji’s additions, including the Alai Darwaza, to 1296–1311. The opening dates the tower to the early 13th century and the Alai Darwaza to 1311. Those statements are not reconciled. This window runs from the 1199 start to the 1311 gate. It is not a claim of continuous building, and it does not adopt 1503 as an end.
records.summary: The tower, mosque and gates a few kilometres south of Delhi, associated with the early Delhi sultans.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.locator: Opening; Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis
citations.supports: The place, the early 13th-century tower, the 1311 gate, and the 1199–1503 and 1296–1311 statements.

details.heading: Who built it
details.text: The brief synthesis says the Quwwatu’l-Islam was completed by Qutb ud din Aibak and Shamsu’d-Din Iltutmish, and that Alauddin Khalji added the Alai Darwaza and a madrasa between 1296 and 1311. The opening says the mosque reused material from some 20 Brahman temples.

citations.supports: Aibak, Iltutmish, Khalji’s dates, and the reused temple material.

records.title: Fatehpur Sikri
records.dateNote: The brief synthesis says Akbar made the city his capital and that it was constructed between 1571 and 1573, and that the capital moved to Lahore in 1585. Criterion (iv) describes the ensemble as constructed between 1571 and 1585. The window follows that ensemble dating. It is not a claim that Akbar ruled only these years. His reign record is separate.
records.summary: Akbar’s planned city in Agra district, capital for a short time in the 1570s and 1580s.
records.locationNote: Converted from the UNESCO property reference N27 5 51.101 E77 39 59.4. The point locates the inscribed city, not the Mughal empire and not Akbar’s movements.

citations.supports: Akbar’s capital, the 1571–1585 building dates, the move in 1585, and the property reference point.

records.title: Rani-ki-Vav at Patan
records.dateNote: The page says the stepwell was initially built as a memorial to a king in the 11th century. The years 1001–1100 are that century’s search window, not a start or completion date. The brief synthesis repeats the 11th-century memorial and names the Maru-Gurjara style. It does not name the king.
records.summary: An 11th-century stepwell on the Saraswati at Patan, built as a memorial and as a water structure.
records.locationNote: Converted from the UNESCO property reference N23 51 32 E72 6 6. The point locates the stepwell, not a kingdom.

citations.supports: The 11th-century memorial, the Saraswati at Patan, the Maru-Gurjara style, and the property reference point.

records.title: Khalji dynasty
records.dateNote: The article dates the dynasty 1290–1320 and calls it the second ruling dynasty of the Delhi sultanate. The last Khalji, Qutb al-Din Mubarak Shah, was murdered in 1320. The window is the dynasty, not a map of every campaign.
records.summary: The second dynasty of the Delhi sultanate, dated 1290–1320, which expanded campaigns into the south.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Delhi is the sultanate’s seat in the article. No coordinate is given, so no point is shown, and no territory is drawn.

citations.supports: The 1290–1320 span, the place in the sultanate, and the murder of the last Khalji in 1320.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Jalal-ud-Din Firuz Khalji, formerly the top commander under the Mamluk dynasty, took the throne after his faction killed Kay-Qubad. He was already elderly. His nephew Juna Khan murdered him in 1296 and reigned as Alauddin Khalji. Qutb al-Din Mubarak Shah, the last Khalji, was murdered in 1320. Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq then began the next dynasty.

citations.supports: The succession from Jalal-ud-Din to Alauddin to Mubarak Shah, and the Tughluq replacement.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: Alauddin reigned 20 years. The article lists the capture of Ranthambhor in 1301, Chitor in 1303, Mandu in 1305, and the annexation of Devagiri. Malik Kafur’s southern expedition of 1308 is said to have taken Warangal, overthrown the Hoysalas south of the Krishna, and occupied Madura. He returned to Delhi in 1311. These are campaign claims, not borders.

citations.supports: The 20-year reign and the named campaigns.

records.title: Jalal-ud-Din Firuz Khalji
records.dateNote: The dynasty is dated from 1290, and the article says his nephew murdered him in 1296. The day of either event is not given. For a time he was so unpopular that he dared not enter the capital.
records.summary: Founder of the Khalji dynasty at Delhi, killed by his nephew in 1296.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is given, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The founding, the reluctance to enter the capital, and the murder in 1296.

records.title: Alauddin Khalji
records.dateNote: He took the title after murdering his uncle in 1296 and reigned 20 years. The article says he died in early 1316. The year 1316 is that early death, not a day. Campaigns named in the article are not drawn as borders.
records.summary: Khalji sultan from 1296, whose campaigns reached Rajasthan, Malwa and the Deccan.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is given for the sultan or for a capital point, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The 1296 accession, the 20-year reign, the early 1316 death, and the named campaigns.

records.title: Tipu Sultan
records.dateNote: The article says he reigned from December 1782 until his death on 4 May 1799, when Seringapatam was stormed. The search years are 1782 and 1799. He was born on 1 December 1751; an earlier birth date of 20 November 1750 is noted as superseded. Birth is not the start of the reign.
records.summary: Sultan of Mysore from December 1782, killed when the British stormed Seringapatam in 1799.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point from the English Wikipedia article coordinates, accessed 12 November 2026. It locates the present place named by the historical source. It is not an ancient survey and not a boundary.

citations.locator: Opening and the account of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War
citations.supports: The reign dates, the death on 4 May 1799, and Seringapatam as the capital.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: He was the son of Hyder Ali, who had become ruler of Mysore after ousting the Wodeyar rulers. Tipu succeeded when his father was killed during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, and he took the title of sultan in 1784 with the Treaty of Mangalore.

citations.supports: Hyder Ali, the succession in December 1782, and the 1784 title.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: He fought in the Anglo-Mysore wars. The Treaty of Seringapatam in March 1792 required him to cede half his dominions, pay an indemnity, and give two sons as hostages. In 1799 British-led forces stormed the capital and he was killed in the breach. The ceded half is not given a map here.

citations.supports: The 1792 treaty and the 1799 storm.

details.heading: Culture and religion
details.text: The article describes administrative reforms, new coins, the Mauludi calendar, and Mysorean rockets. It also reports forced conversions of some non-Muslim communities and, on the other hand, grants to Hindu temples and letters to the pontiff of Sringeri. Those reports are left side by side.

citations.supports: The reforms, the rockets, the conversions, and the temple grants.

records.title: Salt March
records.dateNote: Gandhi set out on 12 March 1930 and reached Dandi on 5 April. He and his followers took salt on 6 April. The article says this was the first act of a larger civil-disobedience campaign that extended into early 1931. Gandhi was released in January 1931, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931. The window covers the march and that campaign, not every day of protest.
records.summary: Gandhi’s march from Sabarmati to Dandi against the British salt monopoly, and the civil disobedience that followed.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article names Sabarmati near Ahmadabad and Dandi near Surat, and a distance of about 240 miles. It does not give a coordinate, so no point is shown. The route is not drawn.

citations.locator: Opening and the narrative of the march
citations.supports: The dates, the route, the salt laws, and the campaign into early 1931.

details.heading: Events
details.text: The salt laws stopped Indians producing or selling salt and required them to buy taxed salt. On 6 April 1930 the marchers picked up salt at Dandi. Gandhi was arrested in early May. On 21 May Sarojini Naidu led a march on the Dharasana saltworks, where police beat marchers. By the end of 1930 about 60,000 people were in jail.

citations.locator: Narrative of the march and its aftermath
citations.supports: The law, the 6 April act, the arrests, Dharasana, and the jail figure as stated.

details.heading: What this was not
details.text: The march did not end British rule. Independence in 1947 is a separate record. Gandhi is not listed as a ruler.

citations.supports: The march as civil disobedience against British rule, not as a transfer of sovereignty.

records.title: Bimbisara
records.dateNote: Britannica gives Bimbisara of the Haryanka line a reign of about 543 to about 491 BCE. Both ends are approximate. The years are 543 and 491 BCE, stored as -543 and -491 because the atlas has no year 0.
records.summary: Haryanka king of Magadha who added the kingdom of Anga.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article places Magadha in what is now west-central Bihar and does not give a coordinate for Bimbisara, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The Haryanka reign of about 543–491 BCE and the addition of Anga.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: Under Bimbisara, Anga in eastern Bihar was added to Magadha. The article says Kosala was annexed later, without naming the king of that annexation.

citations.supports: Anga under Bimbisara and a later annexation of Kosala.

records.title: Early Magadha
records.dateNote: The Magadha article says the kingdom was important from the 6th century BCE. The year 599 BCE only opens that century’s search window. It is not a foundation date. The end, about 325 BCE, is the year the Chandragupta article gives for his taking the throne of Magadha. Nanda rule in the 4th century BCE sits inside this window and is not given its own kings here. The later Gupta use of Magadha is a separate record.
records.summary: The Ganges kingdom that was the base of the Haryanka and Nanda lines before Chandragupta.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article places Magadha in present west-central Bihar and names Pataliputra as a later imperial capital. No coordinate is copied for this early kingdom, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The 6th-century importance, the Haryanka and Nanda succession, and the Ganges setting.

citations.locator: Narrative of the rise to power
citations.supports: Chandragupta’s taking the Magadha throne about 325 BCE as the end of this earlier record.

records.title: Maurya empire
records.dateNote: The Chandragupta article dates his reign about 321 to about 297 BCE and says he began the dynasty. The Shunga article says Pushyamitra replaced the Mauryan dynasty about 185 BCE. The window joins those two statements. It is not a claim that one border lasted the whole time. Ashoka’s own dates are a separate record and are given in two conflicting ranges.
records.summary: The dynasty begun by Chandragupta and ended, on the Shunga article’s dating, when Pushyamitra replaced the last Maurya about 185 BCE.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point for Pataliputra from the English Wikipedia article coordinates. Britannica names Pataliputra as the imperial capital of the dynasties based in Magadha. The point is not a Mauryan survey and not the empire’s border. The coloured sheet, when the year is near 300 or 200 BCE, is the separate historical-basemaps drawing.

citations.supports: The dynasty’s beginning and the reign of about 321–297 BCE.
Pushyamitra’s replacement of the Mauryan dynasty about 185 BCE.
Pataliputra as the imperial capital of the Mauryan dynasty.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: Chandragupta founded the line. His son Bindusara is said to have continued the expansion south. The Chandragupta article does not give Bindusara’s years, so Bindusara is not given a separate dated record. Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta and son of Bindusara, is the third emperor and has his own record.

citations.supports: Bindusara as son and successor, without regnal years.

citations.locator: Top question on coming to power
citations.supports: Ashoka as third emperor, grandson of Chandragupta and son of Bindusara.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: Chandragupta’s empire is described as reaching from the Himalayas and the Kabul valley to the Vindhya Range. The Magadha article says that under the Mauryas the empire included almost the entire subcontinent. Those are the articles’ extent claims, not a polygon drawn for this project. The map colour comes only from the dated historical-basemaps sheet.

citations.supports: The Himalaya-to-Vindhya description.
The claim of an almost subcontinental Mauryan empire.

details.heading: What is not dated here
details.text: Bindusara has no regnal years on the Chandragupta page used here. Two ranges are printed for Ashoka and are left in his own record. No Mauryan border was traced by hand.

citations.supports: Bindusara is named without dates.

records.title: Chandragupta Maurya
records.dateNote: The opening dates the reign about 321 to about 297 BCE. The narrative also says he took the Magadha throne about 325 BCE, won the Punjab about 322, and began the dynasty the following year. Those statements are all kept. The search window follows the opening’s reign pair. He died about 297 BCE at Shravanabelagola.
records.summary: Founder of the Maurya dynasty, reigning about 321 to about 297 BCE.
records.locationNote: Modern reference point for Pataliputra, the Magadha capital named by Britannica, from the English Wikipedia coordinates. It is not the site of his death at Shravanabelagola and not the empire’s border.

citations.locator: Opening and the narrative of 325–321 BCE
citations.supports: The reign of about 321–297 BCE, the Magadha throne about 325, and the start of the dynasty.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: He overthrew the Nanda dynasty, defeated Seleucus in 305 BCE, and held an empire described from the Himalayas and the Kabul valley to the Vindhya Range. Kautilya was his minister. The described extent is not drawn as a private polygon.

citations.supports: The Nanda overthrow, Seleucus in 305 BCE, and the stated extent.

details.heading: Capital
details.text: He ascended the throne of Magadha. The Magadha article names Pataliputra as the imperial capital of the Mauryan dynasty.

citations.supports: Pataliputra as the Mauryan capital.

records.title: Ashoka
records.dateNote: The opening gives the reign as about 265–238 BCE and also as about 273–232 BCE. The death is printed as 238? BCE. The search window follows the first pair only so the two ranges are not silently merged. The second pair is still visible in the label. He conquered Kalinga in the eighth year of his reign. With his death the article says the empire disintegrated.
records.summary: Third Maurya emperor, whose reign the same article dates in two different ways, and who renounced armed conquest after Kalinga.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. His edicts are at many sites. No single coordinate is used, so no point is shown, and no territory is drawn beyond the dated historical-basemaps sheet.

citations.supports: The two reign ranges, the uncertain death year, and the Kalinga conquest.

details.heading: Dynasty
details.text: He was the grandson of Chandragupta and the son of Bindusara, and the third Maurya emperor. After Bindusara’s death he and his brothers fought a succession war.

citations.locator: Top question on coming to power
citations.supports: Parentage and the succession war.

details.heading: Reign
details.text: He conquered Kalinga, modern Odisha, in his eighth year, then renounced armed conquest and ruled through what he called dharma. The article says the empire disintegrated at his death. Neither range is treated as a border.

citations.supports: Kalinga, the turn from conquest, and the disintegration at his death.

details.heading: Culture and religion
details.text: He patronised Buddhism, stupas, monasteries, and rock and pillar edicts, and the article reports missions that included his son and daughter sent to Sri Lanka. He also urged respect among sects. These are religious and administrative claims, not a map.

citations.supports: The edicts, the patronage, and the Sri Lanka mission as reported.

records.title: Shunga dynasty
records.dateNote: Pushyamitra founded the house about 185 BCE. If the Puranic account is followed, the article says Shunga rule lasted 112 years and ended about 73 BCE. The article flags that most accounts of the reign are late and that the total depends on the Puranas. The window uses those approximate ends.
records.summary: The house that replaced the Mauryas about 185 BCE and, on the Puranic count, ended about 73 BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article names Pataliputra, Ayodhya, and Vidisha among the cities. It does not give one coordinate, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The foundation about 185 BCE, the 112-year Puranic tenure, and the end about 73 BCE.

records.title: Pushyamitra
records.dateNote: He founded the dynasty about 185 BCE by assassinating Brihadratha, the last Maurya. The article says he ruled for roughly 36 years. The end year 149 BCE is 185 minus 36, using those approximate figures. It is not an independently recorded death date. Later Shunga history is described as largely uncertain.
records.summary: Founder of the Shunga house, who replaced the last Maurya about 185 BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is given, so no point is shown.

citations.locator: Opening and the paragraph on the length of the reign
citations.supports: The assassination about 185 BCE and a reign of roughly 36 years.

records.title: Bindusara
records.dateNote: The article calls him the second Mauryan emperor and gives a reign of c. 297 to c. 273 BCE. He was a son of Chandragupta and the father of Ashoka. Greco-Roman writers call him Amitrochates or Amitraghata. The dates are the article’s approximate reign, not a dated inscription.
records.summary: Second Mauryan emperor, reigning between Chandragupta and Ashoka on the article’s approximate dates.
records.locationNote: The point is the modern Wikipedia coordinate for Pataliputra, the Mauryan capital already used for Chandragupta. It is a reference point, not a boundary.

citations.supports: The second Mauryan emperor, son of Chandragupta and father of Ashoka, with a reign given as c. 297 to c. 273 BCE.

records.title: Kanva dynasty
records.dateNote: The article dates the dynasty to 73–28 BCE and says Vasudeva Kanva overthrew the Shunga ruler Devabhuti. Puranas name Pataliputra, while the article says the coins concentrate around Vidisha. No outline is drawn.
records.summary: The short-lived house that replaced the Shungas, dated by the article to 73–28 BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article does not settle a single capital between the Puranic Pataliputra and the coins around Vidisha, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The dynasty’s dates 73–28 BCE, Vasudeva Kanva’s overthrow of Devabhuti, and the Pataliputra versus Vidisha evidence.

records.title: Kharavela
records.dateNote: The article calls him an emperor of Kalinga in the 2nd or 1st century BCE. It says the only source is the Hathigumpha inscription, which is undated and partly illegible. This window is that two-century span. It is not a measured reign, and no year inside it is a dated event.
records.summary: Ruler of Kalinga known from the undated Hathigumpha inscription, placed by the article in the 2nd or 1st century BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The inscription does not supply a coordinate, so no point and no outline are shown.

citations.supports: An emperor of Kalinga in the 2nd or 1st century BCE, known from the undated and partly illegible Hathigumpha inscription.

records.title: Indo-Greek kingdoms
records.dateNote: The article says the kingdom was founded when the Graeco-Bactrian king Demetrius I invaded India from Bactria in about 200 BC, and that the name covers several Hellenistic states with capitals including Taxila, Sagala, Pushkalavati and Bagram. The lead does not give one end year, so this record is only the foundation year. A later sentence about Western Satraps lingering to 415 CE is not used as an end date.
records.summary: Hellenistic kingdoms in the northwest, founded about 200 BCE when Demetrius I invaded from Bactria.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The article names several capitals and does not give one coordinate, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Hellenistic states in the northwest, and a foundation about 200 BC when Demetrius I invaded from Bactria.

records.title: Chera dynasty, early evidence
records.dateNote: The article says the Cheras are documented as early as the third century BCE and names them as one of the three crowned kings of Tamilakam, with the Cholas and the Pandyas. The window is that century. It is not a continuous reign, and it does not replace the existing 1–300 CE Chera record.
records.summary: One of the three crowned houses of Tamilakam, documented as early as the third century BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is taken from the article, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Documentation as early as the third century BCE, and the Cheras as one of the three crowned kings of Tamilakam.

records.title: Early Cholas
records.dateLabel: 600 BCE–300 CE in the article; this record is the BCE part
records.dateNote: The Early Cholas article gives the pre- and post-Sangam window as 600 BCE–300 CE, with capitals at Urayur (Tiruchirappalli) and Kaveripattinam, and says written records are scarce. This record keeps only the BCE part so it can be found on the early timeline. The existing early Chola record still covers 1–300 CE. Neither record is a territorial outline.
records.summary: The early Chola house, whose article dates the scarce written record from 600 BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The named capitals are not given a coordinate here, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: A Sangam window given as 600 BCE–300 CE, capitals at Urayur and Kaveripattinam, and scarce written records.

records.title: Pandya dynasty, early evidence
records.dateNote: The article says the dynasty existed since at least the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE, with later imperial phases in the 6th–10th and 13th–14th centuries. This window is only that early span. It is not a claim that one king ruled the whole of it, and it does not replace the existing early Pandya record.
records.summary: The Pandya house, which the article traces back at least to the 5th–3rd centuries BCE.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate is taken from the article, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: A dynasty existing since at least the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE, with later imperial phases named separately.

records.title: Kakatiya dynasty
records.dateNote: The article says the dynasty ruled much of the eastern Deccan in the 12th to 14th centuries, with its capital at Orugallu, now Warangal. Early rulers were feudatories. They assumed sovereignty under Rudradeva in 1163. Ganapati Deva ruled 1199–1262. The article says an attack by Ulugh Khan in 1323 ended in the defeat of the Kakatiya army. The window uses 1163 and that 1323 defeat. The lead was cut off after “the demise of the”, so a later date is not added.
records.summary: Telugu dynasty of Warangal, sovereign from Rudradeva in 1163 until the defeat of 1323.
records.locationNote: The point is the modern Wikipedia coordinate for Warangal, the city identified with the Kakatiya capital Orugallu. It is a reference point, not a boundary.

citations.supports: Capital at Orugallu (Warangal), sovereignty under Rudradeva in 1163, Ganapati Deva’s reign 1199–1262, and the defeat in 1323.

records.title: Paramara dynasty
records.dateNote: The article says the dynasty ruled Malwa and surrounding areas between 948 and 1305. Early rulers were probably Rashtrakuta vassals. Around 972 Siyaka sacked Manyakheta and the house became sovereign, with Dhara as a later capital. Mahalakadeva was defeated and killed by Alauddin Khalji’s forces in 1305. The article adds that epigraphic evidence suggests rule continued for a few years after his death, so 1305 is the dated defeat, not a proven last inscription.
records.summary: The Malwa house dated 948–1305, sovereign after Siyaka’s sack of Manyakheta.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Dhara and Mandu are named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Rule in Malwa from 948 to 1305, sovereignty after the sack of Manyakheta around 972, and Mahalakadeva’s death in 1305.

records.title: Karkota dynasty
records.dateNote: The article dates the dynasty to c. 625–855 CE and says it ruled the Kashmir valley and some northern parts of the subcontinent. Lalitaditya built the Martand Sun Temple. Avanti Varman took the throne in 855 and began the Utpala dynasty. The opening date is the article’s circa.
records.summary: Kashmir dynasty of about 625–855, ended when Avanti Varman founded the Utpala house.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Martand is named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The c. 625–855 dates, rule in the Kashmir valley, Martand, and Avanti Varman’s accession in 855.

records.title: Gujarat Sultanate
records.dateNote: The article says Muzaffar Shah I, governor of Gujarat, declared independence from the Tughlaq dynasty in 1394. Ahmad Shah I moved the capital to Ahmedabad in 1411. The article says the sultanate ended in 1573, when Akbar annexed it. A short restoration after 1583 is described and is not given a separate end year here.
records.summary: The western sultanate founded in 1394 and annexed by Akbar in 1573.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Ahmedabad is named as the capital from 1411, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Independence in 1394, the move to Ahmedabad in 1411, and annexation by Akbar in 1573.

records.title: Ghurid empire
records.dateNote: The article says the dynasty ruled in Ghor from the 8th century and became an empire from 1175 to 1215. This record uses the empire years only. It says Muhammad of Ghor seized Lahore and expelled the Ghaznavids from their last stronghold. The earlier local chiefdom is not given its own window.
records.summary: The Ghurid empire of 1175–1215, which took Lahore from the Ghaznavids.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Ghor and Lahore are named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: An empire from 1175 to 1215, centered in Ghor, and Muhammad of Ghor’s seizure of Lahore.

records.title: Peshwa
records.dateNote: The article calls the Peshwa the second office of the Maratha Empire (1674–1818), after the Chhatrapati. The office became hereditary when Shahu gave it to Bajirao Ballal. After Shahu I, the Peshwas held the government, and from Balaji Rao they were the supreme authority while the Chhatrapati’s position became nominal. The 1674–1818 span is the article’s span for the empire, not a list of every Peshwa’s years.
records.summary: The Maratha office that became hereditary under Shahu and later the effective government.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Pune is the associated later seat used for browsing. No coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The office in the Maratha Empire of 1674–1818, the hereditary grant to Bajirao Ballal, and the later supremacy of the Peshwas.

records.title: Baji Rao I
records.dateNote: The article says the Peshwa’s office was most powerful under Baji Rao I (r. 1720–1740). Those are the years used here. No extent is drawn.
records.summary: Peshwa under whom the article says the office was at its most powerful, 1720–1740.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The office was most powerful under Baji Rao I, r. 1720–1740.

records.title: Partition of India
records.dateNote: The article says British India was divided into the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan under the Indian Independence Act 1947, and that Bengal and Punjab were divided. The two dominions came into existence at midnight on 14–15 August 1947. This record is that year. It is not a boundary of either new state.
records.summary: The 1947 division of British India into two dominions, with Bengal and Punjab divided.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No outline of the partition is drawn.

citations.supports: The division into two dominions under the Indian Independence Act, the division of Bengal and Punjab, and 14–15 August 1947.

records.title: Integration of the princely states
records.dateNote: The article says India in 1947 included 562 princely states under British suzerainty, and that integrating them into an Indian Union was pursued over the next decade. The window is 1947 through 1957 as that decade. It is not a statute date for every accession, and no state boundary is drawn.
records.summary: The post-1947 effort to bring 562 princely states into the Indian Union.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The states were not one territory, so no outline is drawn.

citations.supports: 562 princely states in 1947, and integration pursued over the following decade.

records.title: States Reorganisation Act, 1956
records.dateNote: The article calls the Act a major reform that organised state boundaries along linguistic lines, in force with the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956. It notes Potti Sreeramulu’s death in 1952 and Andhra State in 1953 as the movement’s turning point. This record is the 1956 Act, not a map of the new states.
records.summary: The 1956 linguistic reorganisation of India’s states.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. The Act’s new boundaries are not drawn.

citations.supports: A linguistic reorganisation in force with the Seventh Amendment in 1956, after Andhra State in 1953.

records.title: Chhattisgarh
records.dateNote: The article says Chhattisgarh was formerly part of Madhya Pradesh and was granted statehood on 1 November 2000, with Raipur as the capital. The window runs to 2026 so the state remains findable. 2026 is the atlas limit, not an end of the state. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956, had placed the region in Madhya Pradesh.
records.summary: State created from Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 2000, with its capital at Raipur.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No state boundary is drawn.

citations.supports: Statehood on 1 November 2000 with Raipur as capital, after being part of Madhya Pradesh.

records.title: Telangana
records.dateNote: The article says the Telangana movement obtained bifurcation with the creation, in 2014, of the state of Telangana. The lead used here does not give the day. The window runs to 2026 so the state remains findable. 2026 is the atlas limit, not an end of the state.
records.summary: State created in 2014 from the Telugu-speaking region described in the article.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No state boundary is drawn.

citations.supports: Creation of the state of Telangana in 2014.

records.title: Shashanka
records.dateNote: The article says historians place his rule between 600 and 636, while other sources place it between 590 and 625, and that the reign lasted approximately from 593 to 636. This window uses the first of those ranges. His capital was Karnasuvarna. No coordinate was taken, so the point is not shown. An approximate traced outline is separate.
records.summary: King of Gauda in the early 7th century, a contemporary of Harsha.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Karnasuvarna is named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Historians place the reign between 600 and 636, with Karnasuvarna as the capital, and name the alternate ranges.

records.title: Chandela empire
records.dateNote: The lead says the empire existed from the early 9th century to the 14th century, with its power base in Jejakabhukti, and that the Chandelas began as feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. It does not give a foundation year. 801 is the start of the 9th century used as the opening of that span, not a dated accession.
records.summary: The Jejakabhukti house the lead dates from the early 9th century to the 14th century.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Khajuraho is the associated place already cited for the temples. This record does not repeat that coordinate.

citations.supports: An empire from the early 9th century to the 14th century, based in Jejakabhukti, beginning as Pratihara feudatories.

records.title: Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty
records.dateNote: The lead says the dynasty ruled parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan between about 940 and about 1244, with its capital at Anahilavada, now Patan. Mularaja supplanted the last Chavda ruler around 940.
records.summary: The Solanki house of Anahilavada, dated by the lead to about 940–1244.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Patan is named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Rule in Gujarat and Rajasthan from about 940 to about 1244, with the capital at Anahilavada (Patan).

records.title: Imperial Eastern Gangas
records.dateNote: The lead divides the dynasty into Early Eastern Gangas (493–1077), Imperial Eastern Gangas (1077–1436) and Khemundi Gangas (1436–1947). This record is the imperial phase, which matches an Odisha-coast drawing. It is not the 20th-century phase.
records.summary: The imperial phase of the Eastern Gangas in Kalinga, 1077–1436.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The imperial phase is given as 1077–1436, after the early phase and before the Khemundi Gangas.

records.title: Sena dynasty
records.dateNote: The lead says Hemanta Sena styled himself king in 1095, Vijaya Sena ruled 1096–1159, and Lakshmana Sena succeeded in 1179. It says Qutbuddin Aibak’s forces campaigned in 1203–1204. The window uses 1095 and that campaign.
records.summary: The Bengal house that followed the Palas, from Hemanta Sena in 1095 to the 1203–1204 campaign.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Nadia is named as a later capital, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Hemanta Sena in 1095, Vijaya Sena’s reign 1096–1159, and the 1203–1204 campaign.

records.title: Seuna (Yadava) dynasty
records.dateNote: The lead dates the Yadavas of Devagiri to about 1187–1317 and says the kingdom was annexed by the Khalji dynasty of Delhi in 1308. The window follows the lead’s span. 1308 is the annexation year stated there, not a replacement for 1317.
records.summary: The Devagiri house the lead dates to about 1187–1317.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Devagiri is named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: The Yadavas of Devagiri, about 1187–1317, annexed by the Khaljis in 1308.

records.title: Later Pandyas
records.dateNote: The lead says the dynasty had a later imperial phase in the 13th and 14th centuries, and that in the second half of the 13th century it ruled territories in south India and northern Sri Lanka through vassals of Madurai. This window is that phase. It does not replace the earlier Pandya records.
records.summary: The later imperial Pandyas of Madurai, placed by the lead in the 13th and 14th centuries.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. Madurai is named, but no coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: A later imperial phase in the 13th and 14th centuries, including northern Sri Lanka under vassals of Madurai.

records.title: Malwa Sultanate
records.dateNote: The lead says Dilawar Khan made Malwa independent in 1401 and that the sultanate was conquered from Baz Bahadur in 1562. This is not the Delhi Khalji house.
records.summary: The Malwa sultanate from Dilawar Khan in 1401 to the conquest of 1562.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Independence in 1401 and the conquest from Baz Bahadur in 1562.

records.title: Gajapati empire
records.dateNote: The lead says the empire reigned from about 1434 to 1541, founded by Kapilendra Deva after Bhanu Deva IV, with its capital at Kataka.
records.summary: The Odisha kingdom founded by Kapilendra Deva, about 1434–1541.
records.locationNote: The point is the coordinate on the English Wikipedia article for the Gajapati Empire, accessed 12 November 2026. It is a reference point, not a boundary.

citations.supports: A reign from about 1434 to 1541, founded by Kapilendra Deva, with the capital at Kataka.

records.title: Bijapur Sultanate
records.dateNote: The lead says Bijapur became independent of the Bahmanis in 1490 and was conquered by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1686.
records.summary: The Adil Shahi sultanate of Bijapur, independent in 1490 and conquered in 1686.
records.locationNote: Timeline-only record. No coordinate was taken, so no point is shown.

citations.supports: Independence from the Bahmanis in 1490 and the Mughal conquest in 1686.
